# Condensed Nearest Neighbor {#sec-imbalenced-cnn}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Condensed Nearest Neighbor
:::

Condensed Nearest Neighbor (CNN) uses an iterative approach to decide which observations to remove [@hart1968cnn].
This makes the method an undersampling/downsampling method.

[Downsampling](imbalenced-downsample.qmd) by itself can remove informative observations as that method doesn't the method indiscriminately removes observations.
CNN is based on trying to avoid this mistake.
By trying to create a subset of the majority class that keeps enough information in it to correctly classify all the observations in the original data set.
Or said differently,
CNN tries to remove only observations from the majority class that can be removed without influencing the performance.

This method is another method that cares about the decision boundary.
The rationale is that we can remove observations from inside each class distribution,
leaving the boundary points.
This method can be seen as a data reduction method.
We make it into an undersampling method by only applying it to the majority classes,
but the method itself doesn't actually care whether it is working with a majority or minority class.

The method works on a class-by-class basis,
Typically, only affecting the majority (missing: class), and the general algorithm goes like this:

Start by setting up two buckets, **store** and **grabbag**.

1. You place a single observation into the store.
2. Then you look at the remaining samples and try to classify them using the observations in store as a reference set using a 1-nearest neighbour classifier. If an observation is missclassified, then it is moved into the store; it is moved to the grabbag.
3. Now loop through the grabbag, and try to classify them using the store as the reference set. Any misclassified observations are moved into the store.
4. Repeat 3 until either grabbag is empty or a complete run of 3. Doesn't move any observation from grabbag to store.
5. Discard any observation in the grabbag. The observations in store are the consistent subset.

What is important from this algorithm is that it produces a consistent subset of the data set.
This doesn't mean that it is the smallest possible one,
just that it can generate it consistently.
However, the set is order dependent as the algorithm will produce different results depending on which observations are first put in the store.

What we notice is that points that are deeply inside a given class will be correctly classified by their neighbors,
and will thus be discarded.
On the other hand, points near the decision boundaries are more likely to be misclassified,
and thus more likely to be kept.

If the classes overlap a lot, then we won't be able to discard that many points,
And if the classes cleanly separate, then we should be able to discard most of the observations.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_cnn()`.

```{r}
#| label: step_cnn
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_cnn(MS_Zoning) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

The majority class was cut down sharply, from more than two thousand observations to a few hundred.
The minority class was left alone, which is what we want from an under-sampling method.

Recall from the description above that the result depends on which observation is seeded into the store first, and on the order in which the remaining observations are scanned.
Both are random, so running the step with a different seed gives a different answer.

```{r}
#| label: step_cnn-seeds
cnn_with_seed <- function(seed) {
  recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
    step_cnn(MS_Zoning, seed = seed) |>
    prep() |>
    bake(new_data = NULL) |>
    count(MS_Zoning) |>
    mutate(seed = seed)
}

bind_rows(cnn_with_seed(1), cnn_with_seed(2), cnn_with_seed(3))
```

The counts move around between runs.
This is worth keeping in mind, because it means the size of the data set you get out is not something you can set in advance the way you can with the sampling methods.
It is a consequence of the algorithm rather than a parameter.

## Python Examples

```{python}
#| label: python-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)
```

We are using the same subset of the `ames` data set as above.

```{python}
#| label: show-data-py
from feazdata import ames

ames_imbalance = ames[ames["MS_Zoning"].isin(
    ["Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density"])]

X = ames_imbalance[["Lot_Area", "Year_Built", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath"]]
y = ames_imbalance["MS_Zoning"]

y.value_counts()
```

{imblearn} provides `CondensedNearestNeighbour()`.

```{python}
#| label: condensednearestneighbour
from imblearn.under_sampling import CondensedNearestNeighbour

X_res, y_res = CondensedNearestNeighbour(random_state=1234).fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

The order dependence is present here as well, but it is much less pronounced.
Rather than comparing counts, we look at which rows were kept, using the `sample_indices_` attribute.

```{python}
#| label: condensednearestneighbour-seeds
import pandas as pd

kept = {}
for seed in [1, 2, 3]:
    cnn = CondensedNearestNeighbour(random_state=seed)
    cnn.fit_resample(X, y)
    kept[seed] = set(cnn.sample_indices_)

pd.DataFrame([
    {"seed": seed, "n_kept": len(rows),
     "shared_with_seed_1": len(rows & kept[1])}
    for seed, rows in kept.items()
])
```

The selected rows do change from seed to seed, so the method is order dependent in both implementations.
But where {themis} swings by a dozen or more observations, {imblearn} settles on the same number every time and differs by only a row or two in which ones it picks.
The two packages are making different choices about how the store is seeded and scanned, and those choices are not part of the published algorithm.
If the size of the resulting data set matters to you, this is a good reason to check it rather than assume it.

This method is also noticeably slower than the others in this section.
It is iterative, and each pass runs a nearest neighbor search against a store that keeps growing, so the cost climbs quickly with the size of the data set.
